name: Change Management
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Hardest Fork Is Organizational: Managing the Human Side of Adoption
lesson.summary: Blockchain projects fail more often from resistance to changed workflows than from broken cryptography, which is why change management, a discipline for guiding people through disruption, matters as much as the technical design.
lesson.body:
Introducing a shared ledger into an organization does not just add a new system to the technology stack. It rewrites who has to trust whom, who no longer gets to be the gatekeeper of a record, and whose job changes shape. A reconciliation clerk whose entire role was resolving disagreements between two companies' ledgers has a very different relationship with a shared, tamper-evident ledger than a manager evaluating it purely on cost savings. Change management is the discipline, developed well before blockchain existed, for guiding people and organizations through exactly this kind of disruption deliberately rather than hoping it sorts itself out.

Two widely used frameworks are worth knowing because they describe the problem from complementary angles. John Kotter's eight-step model treats change as an organizational campaign: create urgency, build a coalition powerful enough to drive the change, craft and communicate a clear vision, remove obstacles, generate short-term wins, and only then lock the new way of working into the culture so it does not quietly revert. The ADKAR model, by contrast, tracks the individual: a person has to move through Awareness of why change is needed, Desire to support it, Knowledge of how to work the new way, Ability to actually do it, and Reinforcement so the old habit does not creep back once attention moves elsewhere. A rollout can satisfy Kotter's organizational checklist and still fail if a single frontline team never gets past the Awareness stage on ADKAR's individual scale.

This is exactly where the cognitive biases covered earlier in the course stop being abstract psychology and start being the actual obstacle. Status quo bias means people will judge the new shared ledger against an inflated, idealized memory of the old process rather than against how the old process actually performed with all its errors and delays. Loss aversion means the clerk who loses gatekeeping authority will weigh that loss more heavily than colleagues weigh the efficiency gained elsewhere in the organization, even if the net benefit to the company is clearly positive. Sunk cost thinking can run in the opposite direction too, once a blockchain pilot is underway: having already invested budget and reputation in it, stakeholders may resist honest evidence that it should be scaled back or shut down, a bias the pilot program and decision framework chapters later in this course build in explicit safeguards against.

Stakeholder analysis, covered as its own concept, is the tool that identifies who is affected and how much power and interest they hold. Change management is what you do with that map once you have it: sequencing communication and training so the people with the most influence and the most to lose are engaged early rather than informed after the decision is final, building in visible short-term wins so support does not erode during the long stretch before full benefits appear, and treating resistance as a signal to investigate rather than an obstacle to route around. A blockchain project with elegant smart contracts and a broken change management plan will still fail, because the ledger only reflects agreements that people are willing to actually make.
